What the new local content policy will mean for Namibian business

By the Katelago HR team

Cabinet approved the National Upstream Petroleum Local Content Policy on 4 August 2026. It has been a long road: approval to develop the policy in 2022, drafts in 2023 and 2025, consultations across all fourteen regions through 2025, and an approval in principle in April 2026.

So what changes on Monday morning? Honestly, not much. What changes over the next three years is a great deal, and the businesses that prepare in the quiet period are the ones that will be ready.

First, what it is not

The policy has not been gazetted. Gazetting is the step that gives an instrument legal force, and until that happens no operator carries a binding obligation under it. The approved text has also not been released publicly, and no percentage targets have been made public.

A policy of this kind does not carry fines or criminal penalties. Its purpose is to guide. Government has said legislation will follow, and the labour ministry confirmed in August 2026 that a legislative framework is needed. As at the date of this guide, no bill had been introduced.

Do not let anyone sell you compliance with something that is not yet in force

There will be consultants offering local content compliance packages in the coming months. Ask them, politely, which legal instrument they are certifying you against. If the answer is the policy, the honest position is that it is not law yet. What you can genuinely prepare is your workforce, your records and your Affirmative Action standing, all of which will be needed whichever form the legislation takes.

What is likely to be required, and who it will touch

Based on the published draft, the policy works through the operators. Operators will be required to prepare a local content plan at petroleum agreement stage, and again when they submit a field development plan, and then report annually against what they promised.

That matters even if you are nowhere near an oil rig. Operators meet local content commitments largely through their supply chain. When an operator has to report on Namibian employment and Namibian procurement, that obligation travels down into every contract it lets, and into every subcontract below that.

So the businesses affected are not only the four or five international operators. They are the logistics firms, the catering companies, the engineering shops, the security providers, the labour suppliers, the accommodation providers and the professional services firms in Walvis Bay, Lüderitz and Windhoek.

The four areas to prepare

1. Namibian employment

The draft policy proposes preference for suitably qualified Namibians, Namibians filling all unskilled positions, and a progressive increase in Namibian representation in professional, technical and managerial roles, phased in after significant discoveries.

Practically, this means you need to be able to answer a simple question in writing: how many of your people are Namibian, at what levels, and what are you doing about the levels where they are not. If that sounds familiar, it is because it is very close to what an Affirmative Action report already asks.

2. Training and skills transfer

The draft treats meaningful training and development as a requirement of operating in the sector, delivered through mentorships, understudies, succession plans and secondments.

Note that word understudy. It is not new. Section 19(3) of the Affirmative Action (Employment) Act already requires a relevant employer to train a Namibian understudy for every non-Namibian it employs. The policy language sits on top of an obligation many employers have never operationalised.

3. Procurement and how contracts are packaged

The draft proposes that contracts be unbundled so that Namibian firms can realistically bid, that opportunities be advertised locally, that tender evaluation weight local value added, and that government maintain a database of pre-qualified local suppliers.

If a supplier database is established, being on it early will matter. Being on it requires the very documents most small Namibian firms are missing: current registration, tax and social security good standing, an Affirmative Action compliance certificate where applicable, and evidence of a real workforce.

4. Ownership

The draft defines a local company as one incorporated in Namibia with at least 51 percent of its equity held by Namibian citizens and its principal place of business in Namibia, and it proposes measures against fronting.

Later reporting suggested a further requirement relating to ownership by previously disadvantaged Namibians. We have not been able to verify that from the policy text itself, so we are not stating it as fact. If ownership structures are something you are considering changing, take advice on the current wording rather than on press reports, including ours.

Be realistic about the timing

There is a lot of excitement, and it is worth grounding it. As at August 2026, no Namibian offshore oil project had taken a final investment decision. The Venus development is the furthest advanced and was described as technically ready, subject to concluding fiscal discussions with government. First oil is a 2029 or 2030 proposition at the earliest.

The Kudu gas to power project may reach a decision sooner. Onshore, testing continues in the Kavango basin. Exploration continues offshore, and one major has already written down a substantial sum on a Namibian licence, which is a useful reminder that not every discovery becomes a development.

What this means for an employer is straightforward. Large scale hiring follows a final investment decision, not a discovery. That gives most Namibian businesses somewhere between two and four years to build genuine capability. That is a gift, provided it is used.

The date to watch is FID

A final investment decision is the moment the joint venture commits the capital. Before it, spending is comparatively small. After it, construction contracts are let and hiring and procurement start in volume. Every workforce plan in this sector should be anchored to an expected FID rather than to a discovery announcement.

My honest read

The risk in a policy like this is that it produces intermediaries rather than industry. That criticism has been made publicly by Namibian economists and it deserves to be taken seriously. A business inserted between an international contractor and a contract, adding a margin and nothing else, does not build a Namibian oil and gas sector. It just makes it more expensive.

The counterweight is capability, and capability is visible. A firm that employs Namibians, trains them properly, keeps its records and can show its compliance is a firm that adds real value. When the reporting obligations arrive and operators start being asked to evidence their local content, that is exactly what they will need from their suppliers.

So the preparation is not really about the policy. It is about being a business worth contracting with. That work can start today and does not need a gazette notice.

What to do in the next ninety days

  1. Confirm whether you are a relevant employer under the Affirmative Action Act, and get your report and compliance certificate current.
  2. Put a real understudy and succession programme in place for every non-Namibian you employ, and keep the training records.
  3. Get your statutory good standing documents current: tax, social security, and registration.
  4. Document your workforce by nationality, occupational level, qualification and training history.
  5. Decide honestly which parts of the supply chain you can actually serve, and build capability there rather than everywhere.
